profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a midsize health-law firm representing a hospital network that wants to publish an internal-to-public white paper on how its legal and compliance teams should use PRISMA 2020 when documenting systematic reviews prepared for policy submissions and litigation-sensitive regulatory responses. The meeting is between the litigation partner supervising publication risk and the senior knowledge management attorney coordinating the drafting process. The agenda is to decide what the final deliverable will include, how the PRISMA 2020 explanation-and-elaboration article will be translated into a legally usable practice document, who will prepare each component, and what timeline will govern circulation before the hospital client's policy committee meets next month. The expected outcome is a shared plan for drafting, internal review, exemplar selection, and circulation of the 'PRISMA guidance pack' for release in time for the committee packet.

members.name: Rachel Kim
members.role: Litigation Partner, Health Regulatory and Evidence Strategy
members.expertise: Healthcare litigation, evidentiary standards, regulatory submissions, publication risk review
members.background: Rachel is a senior partner who advises hospital systems on how published internal methodologies may later be scrutinized in discovery, agency review, and expert challenges; she often converts scientific material into defensible legal process documents.
members.private_state: Rachel wants the project to produce a polished, externally shareable white paper that shows the client has a disciplined evidence-reporting framework without creating discoverable internal commentary that could be used against the hospital later; she is also trying to minimize partner review time next week because she has a trial hearing.
hidden_assumptions: A 'PRISMA guidance pack' naturally means one client-facing white paper plus a short cover memo, not a bundle of working templates and internal training aids.

When people say they will 'map the 27 items,' they mean converting each item into a legally defensible reporting expectation with cautionary notes, not reproducing every explanatory bullet from the article.
The 'examples' to be included should be high-level citations or paraphrased exemplars from published reviews, because reproducing detailed excerpts creates unnecessary permissions and risk issues.
A draft being 'ready for review' means partner-level prose is complete enough to circulate to the client policy committee after one legal scrub.
The 'committee packet deadline' refers to the business-day cutoff when the hospital finalizes materials for distribution, which in practice is 5 p.m. local time two days before the meeting.

members.name: Daniel Ortega
members.role: Senior Knowledge Management Attorney, Clinical Research Support
members.expertise: Research governance, legal operations, knowledge systems, guidance drafting for interdisciplinary teams
members.background: Daniel manages precedent materials and internal guidance for attorneys who support research offices and IRBs; he regularly turns external standards into operational checklists, training slides, and annotated templates for internal users.
members.private_state: Daniel wants this project to become a reusable internal toolkit that demonstrates the value of knowledge management and reduces repeated ad hoc advice requests from research teams; he is also concerned that a thin white paper will be ignored by staff unless it includes concrete drafting aids.
hidden_assumptions: A 'PRISMA guidance pack' obviously includes a practice note, a clause-by-clause checklist, and an annotated template or intake aid for lawyers and compliance analysts.
To 'map the 27 items' means preserving the article's explanation-and-elaboration logic item by item, including the practical bullet points that users can apply directly.
Including 'examples' means inserting short quoted excerpts from published reviews under each PRISMA item so users can see what compliant reporting looks like in context.
A draft being 'ready for review' means a substantively complete working draft that reviewers can mark up for structure, examples, and formatting before final polishing.
The 'committee packet deadline' is the electronic upload cutoff at the end of the stated date, which he treats as effectively end-of-day unless told otherwise.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree to prepare a 'PRISMA guidance pack' for the client.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 understands this as a concise external white paper with a brief transmittal memo, suitable for limited outside circulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 understands this as a broader internal toolkit: practice note, detailed checklist, annotated template, and possibly training aids bundled together.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal planning conversations, 'guidance pack' sounds like an ordinary umbrella term, and both roles routinely use bundle language without listing every component unless a budget or filing rule forces specificity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will 'map the 27 PRISMA items' into the draft.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means distilling each checklist item into a short legal-practice implication and identifying where the final white paper addresses it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means building a near-complete item-by-item operational crosswalk based on the explanation-and-elaboration article's reporting bullets and exemplars.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The verb 'map' is a familiar but elastic knowledge-management term; both hear a plausible professional shorthand and do not feel a need to unpack the level of granularity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the draft should include 'examples from published reviews' so users can see what good reporting looks like.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 will consider the requirement satisfied if the white paper cites a few reviews and briefly describes why they are useful illustrations, avoiding long extracts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 will consider the requirement satisfied only if each major PRISMA section has embedded excerpted sample language or closely reproduced text snippets from published reviews.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are aligned on the abstract purpose of exemplars, and in professional writing meetings 'include examples' often passes without discussion because the dispute is not whether to include them but what level of concreteness makes them usable.

misalignment_points.topic: Interpretation of 'ready for review' by the committee deadline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on having a draft 'ready for review' before the committee packet deadline.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes a polished near-final draft must reach her by 5 p.m. local time on the hospital's packet-finalization day so she can do a quick legal scrub before external circulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes a substantively complete but still rough draft can be uploaded by end-of-day on the stated deadline and then refined after comments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced with internal review cycles and assume the institutional process is already mutually understood; because they use the same deadline language, neither notices the embedded assumptions about finish level and exact cutoff.

turns.inner_thought: We need one clean external-facing white paper with a short cover memo, anchored to PRISMA 2020 but not bloated with internal drafting debris. If this is polished enough, the client can show a disciplined evidence-reporting framework without generating discoverable side commentary. I also need to keep my own review burden contained next week because of the hearing.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. We need a PRISMA guidance pack tied closely to the explanation-and-elaboration article so the hospital has something usable before next month's policy committee meeting.

turns.inner_thought: Good. This should be more than a short paper; it should become a reusable internal toolkit people can actually work from. If we translate all 27 PRISMA items into practical drafting support, legal and compliance teams may stop coming back for one-off advice every time a review writeup appears.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The opportunity is to take the 27-item PRISMA 2020 material and turn it into something practical for the legal and compliance teams handling these systematic-review writeups.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the front-end narrative: why transparent reporting supports defensibility, credibility, and decision making. Daniel can map the 27 items into the draft by translating each into a concise reporting expectation and noting where it's addressed. I do not want a sprawling reproduction of the article.
turns.utterance: Why don't we split it this way: you map the 27 PRISMA items into the draft, and I'll take the front-end framing on why transparent reporting matters for defensibility and decision making.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll build a real item-by-item map using the explanation-and-elaboration article's reporting bullets and exemplars, so users can follow the PRISMA logic directly. That gives us a solid operational crosswalk instead of a thin summary.
turns.utterance: That works. I can build the item-by-item map using the article's reporting bullets and exemplars so users can work from the PRISMA logic directly.

turns.inner_thought: We should have examples, but only at a high level. A few published reviews, cited or briefly paraphrased, will show what good methods reporting looks like without stuffing the piece with copied language or permissions headaches.
turns.utterance: And I do want the draft to include examples from published reviews, especially ones that show clear methods reporting without overloading the document.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, examples are what make these materials usable. I'll pull short quoted excerpts from published reviews for the major sections so readers can see compliant reporting in context. That will make the guidance pack much more concrete.
turns.utterance: Definitely. Examples will make the pack usable, and I'll pull representative published-review language for the main sections so readers can see what good reporting looks like.

turns.inner_thought: I'll write the opening white-paper narrative and the legal caveats at the end. Daniel can assemble the PRISMA mapping and whatever support sits behind it. As long as what comes to me can be folded quickly into one polished client-facing piece, that's fine.
turns.utterance: Then I'll draft the opening white-paper narrative and the final legal caveats, and you can assemble the PRISMA mapping and supporting materials.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll put the checklist structure and annotated user-facing components behind her narrative so the whole guidance pack feels complete and reusable. This is a good chance to show KM can deliver more than a memo.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I can package the checklist structure and annotated user-facing components behind your narrative so the guidance pack feels complete.

turns.inner_thought: The critical point is timing: I need a near-final, partner-level draft in my hands by 5 p.m. local time on the hospital's packet-finalization day, two business days before the meeting, so I can do one quick legal scrub before it goes out. I do not have bandwidth for a rough assembly.
turns.utterance: The key for me is having a draft ready for review before the committee packet deadline next week so I can move it through quickly.

turns.inner_thought: That's manageable. I can have a substantively complete working draft by end of day on the stated deadline, upload it, and then tighten structure, formatting, and any open spots once comments start coming back. That's what ready for review usually means at this stage.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can have a full working draft ready by the packet deadline, then polish formatting and any gaps after comments come back.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll keep my role narrow: narrative and legal scrub. Daniel is taking the PRISMA map, the examples, and the rest of the pack. As long as I get a polished enough draft, I can do a quick pass and send it on without sinking more time into it.
turns.utterance: Great. So I have the narrative and legal scrub, and you handle the PRISMA map, the examples, and the rest of the guidance pack.

turns.inner_thought: Understood. I'll circulate the mapped draft and supporting materials on that timeline. The only likely issue is sourcing the published examples I want to use under each main section, but otherwise this should come together well.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll circulate the mapped draft and supporting materials on that timeline, and I'll flag only if I run into a sourcing issue with the published examples.
